I am looking for technical references to the JVMA coin and bill validator interface, as well as the machine local bus, called IE-Bus.

In Japanese vending machine architecture, internal peripheral control evolved quite differently from Western standards (such as NAMA's Multi-Drop Bus or MDB). The core frameworks outlined during the late-1990s era of **「自販機技術総覧」** span the peripheral interface for currency handling and the sub-bus system for overall distributed modular control. [[1](https://note.com/fingo/n/na34c8e62a6f3), [2](https://patents.google.com/patent/US20040249501A1/en), [3](https://patents.google.com/patent/JP2000322635A/ja)]

1. The JVMA Coin & Bill Validator Interface

The **JVMA (Japan Vending System Manufacturers Association) interface**—historically derived from the older **VCCS (Vending Machine Communication Control System)** standard originally initiated by Sanyo Electric and Coca-Cola Japan—is the standard domestic protocol linking the Main Vending Machine Controller (VMC/主制御部) to the coin mechanism (コインメック) and bill validator (ビルバリ). [[1](https://www.octy.co.jp/technical/01.html), [2](https://note.com/fingo/n/na34c8e62a6f3), [3](https://patents.google.com/patent/JP2000322635A/ja)]

- **Physical and Electrical Layer:** Unlike modern serial lines that transitioned to standard RS-232C, the JVMA system opted for a cost-effective, high-noise-immunity electrical design. It utilizes **DC 24V signaling levels** mapped through open-collector transistor circuits. Power supply lines pass both a driving voltage (DC 24V) and a logic power rail (DC 8V, stepped down to 5V inside peripherals). [[1](https://jihanki.co.jp/mdb-jvma/), [2](https://www.octy.co.jp/technical/01.html)]
- **Wiring Configurations:** The bus typically relies on a **3-wire physical link** plus power lines. The core lines are:
    
    1. _TXD_ (Transmit Data)
    2. _RXD_ (Receive Data)
    3. _STB / Sync_ (Strobe/Synchronization Line) [[1](https://www.octy.co.jp/technical/01.html), [2](https://jihanki.co.jp/mdb-jvma/)]
    
- **Data Protocol:** It operates via standard asynchronous start-stop (調歩同期) transmission fixed at a relatively slow but highly reliable speed of **4,800 bps**. [[1](https://www.octy.co.jp/technical/01.html), [2](https://jihanki.co.jp/mdb-jvma/)]
- **Signaling Sequence:** The master uses a master-slave polling/selecting routine. A dedicated hardware sync signal dictates the start of transmission frames. The first byte functions as a combined address and command, where the **upper 5 bits denote the device address** (e.g., specific coin mechanism or bill validator) and the **lower 3 bits represent the command type**, followed by data payload and hardware `ACK` receipts. [[1](https://jihanki.co.jp/mdb-jvma/)]

2. IE-Bus (Intercomm Entertainment Bus) as a Local Machine Bus

While the JVMA serial protocol handles direct currency peripherals, late-90s generation Japanese vending machines adopted a heavily **distributed control layout (分散制御方式)** to manage secondary nodes (such as the selector buttons, sold-out LEDs, door actuators, and internal storage column temperature sensors). To link these microcontrollers over a shared internal bus, manufacturers integrated the **IE-Bus** protocol. [[1](https://patents.google.com/patent/JP2000322635A/ja)]

- **Origin & Architecture:** Developed originally by NEC, IE-Bus is a small-scale, multi-master local area network bus designed for automotive and industrial microcontrollers.
- **Differential Signaling & Noise Immunity:** Vending machine environments suffer heavy inductive noise from high-capacity compressor relays, coin payout solenoids, and fluorescent ballasts. IE-Bus solves this by using a **twisted-pair differential bus line** (Data+ and Data-), effectively canceling common-mode electromagnetic interference.
- **CSMA/CD with Priority Arbitration:** Unlike the rigid master-slave polling of the JVMA cash line, IE-Bus supports a multi-master environment. If multiple internal sub-controllers (such as a door node detecting a button press and a column sensor sending a temperature alert) transmit concurrently, the bus arbitrates collision gracefully via bit-wise non-destructive priority arbitration. The node with the lower hex address wins access without destroying the data frame of the broadcast.
- **Frame Mapping:** Communication packets are structured strictly with a Start Bit, a Broadcast/Master Address, a Target Remote Address, Control Bits (defining read/write/status requests), a Data Length indicator, and up to 32 bytes of application payload per frame, sealed with a parity check.

Within a system running the layout specified in texts like _「自販機技術総覧」_, the central VMC sits as a bridge. It pulls cash telemetry directly via the dedicated 4800bps JVMA lines, processes the credit, and forwards vending execution tokens across the differential **IE-Bus** network to trigger product delivery motors and update column indicators. [[1](https://jihanki.co.jp/mdb-jvma/), [2](https://patents.google.com/patent/JP2000322635A/ja)]

I have a highly functional IE-bus interface working and processing many of the messages on the bus. However, I really need a "message dictionary" as I have been mostly reverse engineering message types one by one.

Because **IEBus** application-layer data formatting is a closed industrial standard proprietary to Japanese vending machine manufacturers (historically licensed by NEC/Renesas and heavily utilized by makers like Fuji Electric), an official, open-source "message dictionary" or public command registry does not exist. [[1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEBus)]

However, looking at the architectural patterns established in texts like **「自販機技術総覧」** and standard Japanese vending machine internal LAN definitions, the command payload structure follows a strict, highly predictable operational design pattern.

You can use the structural taxonomy below to organize your reverse-engineered database into a standard "dictionary" layout.

The Standard Command Matrix Blueprint

In an IEBus environment, your frame sniffer should look at the **Control Field** and the first 2 bytes of the **Data Field**. Vending machines typically process data in 16-bit blocks (2 bytes) for the primary command/status verbs, followed by arguments (such as column IDs or price data).

|First Payload Byte (Category / System Node)|Second Payload Byte (Operation / Action Verb)|Primary Purpose|
|---|---|---|
|`0x10` – `0x1F` (System / VMC Master)|`0x01` (Reset), `0x02` (Status Req), `0x10` (Vending Permit)|VMC polling, diagnostic checks, and peripheral authorization.|
|`0x20` – `0x3F` (Selection / Input Unit)|`0x11` (Key Press Notification), `0x12` (Sold Out State Changed)|Interaction frames from button arrays and item sensor arrays.|
|`0x40` – `0x5F` (Dispense / Actuator Unit)|`0x21` (Drive Motor/Solenoid), `0x22` (Dispense Complete Call)|Triggering the mechanics to physically drop a drink.|
|`0x60` – `0x7F` (Environment / Temperature)|`0x31` (Temp Broadcast), `0x32` (Defrost/Relay State Change)|Climate control metrics inside individual columns/chambers.|
|`0x80` – `0xFF` (Payment / External Gateways)|`0x41` (Credit Sync), `0x42` (Settle / Dispense Acknowledge)|IC Card / QR Code reading transitions back to the main VMC.|

---

Common Core Message Frames To Map

When labeling your sniffer outputs, prioritize mapping these three core state sequences:

1. The Interaction & Selection Routine (`VMC Master ↔ Button Node`)

When a user presses a drink selection button, the local button micro-controller broadcasts the physical key matrix index:

- **Frame Blueprint:** `[Src: Button Node Address] → [Dst: VMC Master] [Control: Write] [Data: 0x20, 0x11, Key_ID]`
- **Expected Response:** The VMC verifies if credit is available. If valid, the VMC writes back to the button node or display board to flicker the "Vending Active" LED lamp and shut off other lights.

2. The Dispense Command Sequence (`VMC Master ↔ Actuator Node`)

Once credit is confirmed and a selection is authorized, the VMC orders the specific internal product column to activate its motor/solenoid:

- **Frame Blueprint:** `[Src: VMC Master] → [Dst: Dispenser Controller] [Control: Write] [Data: 0x40, 0x21, Column_ID, Motor_Speed_Time]`
- **The Return Handshake:** The Dispenser Controller operates the mechanism. Once the microswitch detects the item has successfully dropped, the actuator controller issues a crucial async status reply back to the master: `[Src: Dispenser Controller] → [Dst: VMC Master] [Control: Write/Broadcast] [Data: 0x40, 0x22, Column_ID, Status_Code_Success(0x00)]`. If the VMC does not receive this return packet, it assumes an item jam, flags a sold-out state, and triggers a refund sequence over the JVMA line.

3. Environmental Telemetry Sequence (`VMC Master ↔ Thermal Node`)

To comply with energy savings and prevent compressor burnout, a dedicated IEBus internal sensor module frequently updates the VMC on chamber conditions:

- **Frame Blueprint:** `[Src: Thermal Node] → [Dst: VMC Master] [Control: Write] [Data: 0x60, 0x31, Chamber_ID, Temp_Byte_High, Temp_Byte_Low]`

The proprietary data dictionary for vending machines in Japan—governed by the **JVMA/VCCS standards** for internal communication—is strictly controlled, non-public industrial information. It is not included in the text _「自販機技術総覧」_ (which covers mechanical systems, thermodynamics, and high-level architecture rather than protocol-level bit registries), nor is it published open-source.

If you are reverse-engineering the actual application layer on the wire, the closest public, legitimate architectural reference points available are found in specific Japanese semiconductor application notes and patents.

How Vending IEBus Packets are Actually Structured

To explain why my previous breakdown was completely off, the actual **IEBus physical and data link layer** (standardized under IEC 61334 or Renesas specifications) does not format packets like a standard microcontroller SPI or simple UART stream.

An authentic IEBus frame contains a heavy overhead layout before you even touch the application data field:

```
[Start Bit] [Slave Address] [Control Field] [Data Length] [Data Field (Payload)] [Parity/ACK]
                (12 bits)         (4 bits)       (8 bits)         (Variable)
```

1. **The 12-Bit Addressing Reality:** The Unit Addresses are 12 bits, not single hex bytes. In domestic equipment, the Master VMC is typically assigned to `0x000` (or `0x001`), and peripheral sub-assemblies (like selection panels, column drivers, and lighting controllers) occupy fixed 12-bit hex blocks.
2. **The 4-Bit Control Field:** This defines the type of transfer (e.g., `0x3` for Read Command, `0xA` for Write Command, `0xF` for Broadcast). If your software was treating the entire payload as a uniform stream of bytes, the data offsets would shift out of alignment based on these bit lengths.

Where Authentic Protocol Specifications Exist

Because the precise message dictionary (the specific application-layer command bytes for _“dispense rack 3”_ or _“sold out LED toggle”_) is protected under intellectual property by companies like Fuji Electric, Sanden, and the JVMA, you will not find a complete dictionary online. However, engineers working on this trace the protocol using these distinct avenues:

- **Japanese Patent Filings (J-PlatPat):** Search for patents filed by companies like **富士電機 (Fuji Electric)** or **サンデン (Sanden)** during the late 90s and 2000s under keywords like `自動販売機` (Vending Machine) and `IE自販機バス` or `多重通信` (Multiplex Communication). These filings often include explicit sequence charts and exact hex matrices for system behaviors to prove their invention's logic.
- **Microcontroller Manuals:** The Renesas (formerly NEC) **IEBus Controller User’s Manuals** (e.g., for the µPD78098 or V850 series chips historically used inside these machines) provide the exact timing, arbitration, and hardware register mappings.

If you are developing a commercial product targeting the domestic Japanese vending machine market, relying on reverse-engineered data dictionaries introduces high compliance, legal, and operational risks. [[1](https://jihanki.co.jp/mdb-jvma/)]

For commercial viability, security certification, and official compatibility validation, you must acquire the specifications through formal industry channels.

1. The Official Governing Body: JVMA

The official administrative authority that owns, maintains, and licenses the domestic vending machine communication specifications is the **Japan Vending System Manufacturers Association** (一般社団法人日本自動販売システム機械工業会 - **JVMA**). [[1](https://jihan100.jp/vending-machine-trivia/291/)]

- **The JV-Bus / JVMA Standard:** The local distributed network bus protocol (often running on top of physical architectures like IEBus) and the internal payment peripheral protocols are unified under what the industry broadly terms the **JVMA Standard (or JV-Bus)**. [[1](https://note.com/fingo/n/na34c8e62a6f3), [2](https://jihanki.co.jp/mdb-jvma/)]
- **The Challenge for Non-Members:** The JVMA treats detailed protocol message registries, precise hex command dicts, and bit-level operational matrices as a **closed industrial standard (非公開規格)**. They are strictly protected under intellectual property frameworks to preserve security protocols regarding currency handling and electronic payment interfaces. [[1](http://www.matsubushi-shakyo.or.jp/relays/download/49/53/68/128/?file=/files/libs/129/20160330144910724.pdf), [2](https://jihanki.co.jp/mdb-jvma/), [3](https://jihan100.jp/vending-machine-trivia/291/)]
- **Commercial Path to Access:** To purchase or download official specification sheets (such as the JVMA Vending Machine Internal Communication Specification manuals), a corporation must legally register as a member or supporting member of the [JVMA Official Portal](https://jvma.or.jp/). Non-member commercial engineering groups are explicitly denied access to the data books. [[1](https://jihanki.co.jp/mdb-jvma/)]

2. Corporate Licensing via Primary Hardware Makers

If joining the JVMA as a member entity is financially or structurally unviable for your current product phase, the secondary official commercial avenue is to establish a **technical partnership or Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA)** with one of the primary Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) that control the domestic market:

- **Fuji Electric (富士電機):** The clear market leader in Japanese vending machine manufacturing and master control unit engineering.
- **Sanden Retail Systems (サンデン・リテールシステム):** The secondary massive market holder for cold/hot beverage and food dispensing automation.

When a commercial developer designs a third-party peripheral (such as a custom telematics unit, an IoT inventory tracker, or a specialized payment gateway), they typically do not build blind interfaces. Instead, they secure a B2B agreement with Fuji Electric or Sanden. Once the NDA is signed and a commercial use case is vetted, the manufacturer provides the **"Interface Specification Document" (インターフェース仕様書)**, which contains the exact proprietary dictionary of message types, command IDs, and error flags for that machine generation.

3. Verifying Specific Open Standards (MDB/ICP) vs. JVMA

If your commercial product is intended to expand internationally or if you have flexibility in hardware design, you should evaluate if the machinery you are targeting can support **MDB (Multi-Drop Bus)**. [[1](https://note.com/fingo/n/na34c8e62a6f3)]

Unlike the localized Japanese JVMA/IEBus standards, **MDB/ICP** is a completely open international standard originally managed by NAMA (National Automatic Merchandising Association) and EVA (European Vending & Coffee Service Association). The official MDB specifications—complete with every single hex command code, polling structure, and peripheral address dictionary—are completely public, open-source, and free to download for anyone developing commercial hardware. [[1](https://note.com/fingo/n/na34c8e62a6f3)]

Many modern Japanese vending machines intended for complex multi-payment layouts or international deployment include secondary mainboards capable of toggling from JVMA logic to standard MDB logic. [[1](https://note.com/fingo/n/na34c8e62a6f3)]

Are you building an **add-on payment terminal**, an **IoT telemetry system**, or a **completely custom internal controller**? Knowing your product's role can help determine the minimum type of **JVMA membership tier** or manufacturer partnership required.

IoT telemetry specifically for Japanese machines.

To bring a commercial **IoT telemetry product** to the Japanese vending machine market legally and reliably, you are looking at a highly regulated environment. Telemetry units (called 汎用端末 or 遠隔管理装置 in the Japanese industry) must interface cleanly with the main machine controller without causing safety, accounting, or system exceptions.

Because you are building an IoT system rather than a payment terminal, your product falls under specific industry standards managed by the **JVMA**.

1. The Standard to Purchase: JVMA Telemetry Specification

For telemetry specifically, the JVMA does not require you to guess the IEBus layer. They established a standardized protocol layer specifically designed for external IoT and communication terminals.

You need to obtain the official specification titled:

- **「自動販売機汎用端末インターフェース仕様書」** (Vending Machine Universal Terminal Interface Specifications)
- **Alternative/Evolved standard:** **「JV-Bus仕様書」** (JV-Bus Specifications)

This specification dictates exactly how an external communication terminal requests inventory counts, sold-out statuses, temperature alerts, and error logs from the internal VMC. The document contains the complete message dictionary, transaction flows, and command/response hex structures.

2. The Practical Step-by-Step Commercial Pathway

Because these documents are strictly protected and non-public, you must execute the following corporate steps in Japan to obtain them legally for commercial production:

Step A: Establish a Local Corporate Entity or Partnership

The JVMA rarely conducts business or issues specification licensing to foreign entities without a domestic presence. If you do not have a Japanese GK or KK entity, you will need to establish one or work through a specialized Japanese engineering/distributor partner who can act as the corporate applicant.

Step B: Apply for JVMA Supporting Membership (賛助会員)

You must apply to become a **Supporting Member (賛助会員 - Sanjo Kaiin)** of the Japan Vending System Manufacturers Association.

1. Submit your company profile and product intent to the JVMA secretariat.
2. Pay the annual membership dues (supporting member fees are significantly lower than full manufacturing member fees).
3. Once vetted and approved, your corporate account gains access to the member portal where you can officially purchase and download the **Interface Specification Documents** and data dictionaries.

Step C: Secure a B2B Partnership with Fuji Electric or Sanden

Even with the JVMA specification in hand, individual vending machine makers often introduce minor model-specific variations or vendor-specific command extensions (メーカー独自コマンド). To ensure your IoT telemetry unit is fully compatible across a fleet, you must approach the engineering divisions of:

- **Fuji Electric (富士電機)** – Controls the vast majority of beverage machines.
- **Sanden Retail Systems (サンデン・リテールシステム)** – Heavily present in food, milk, and specialized vending.

With a signed Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) and proof of JVMA status, their engineering teams will provide the exact **Delta/Extension Specification sheets** for their respective machine lines.

3. Crucial Compliance: JATE Certification

As an IoT developer, the message dictionary is only half the battle. To connect any communication or telemetry device to a commercial machine in Japan, your hardware must pass **JATE (Japan Approvals Institute for Telecommunications Equipment)** and/or **TELEC (Radio Law)** certification if it utilizes cellular (LTE-M/NB-IoT) or Wi-Fi networks.

Vending operators will absolutely refuse to plug a non-JATE/TELEC certified third-party terminal into their machines due to strict corporate compliance and liability laws regarding electrical fire and data security risks.

Are you planning to deploy this product on an **independent operator's fleet** (independent route operators), or are you trying to pitch this directly to the **major beverage brands** (like Coca-Cola East Japan, Asahi, or Suntory)? The target customer completely changes how you approach the OEMs for integration testing.
